name: Testing effect
statement: Retrieving studied material from memory produces better long-term retention than spending the same time studying it again, and learners judge the reverse.
meaning: The comparison that matters is testing against restudying, not testing against nothing. A student who reads a chapter and then tries to recall it, without looking, remembers more a week later than a student who reads it twice. That is a stronger claim than the obvious one about extra exposure, because the restudy condition sees all the material again and the recall attempt only reaches whatever the student can produce. Two features make the effect useful and two make it fragile. It grows with the delay before the final test, and it survives without corrective feedback. It shrinks when the initial recall attempt mostly fails, and it shrinks when the comparison strategy is something more active than rereading. The metacognitive half is the part that behaves like a bias: learners rank rereading above self-testing, and rank it highest exactly where it performs worst.

origin.who: Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke
origin.note: The paper is "Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention", received 4 February 2005 and accepted 24 March 2005. Roediger and Karpicke did not discover the effect and said so, citing Gates in 1917 and Spitzer in 1939, and quoting the title of Glover's 1989 paper, "The 'testing' phenomenon: Not gone but nearly forgotten". What their paper supplied was prose materials, a restudy control and delayed tests.

evidence: Roediger and Karpicke ran two experiments on 120 and 180 Washington University undergraduates. The materials were two passages from a TOEFL preparation book, "The Sun" and "Sea Otters", 256 and 275 words long, each cut into 30 idea units for scoring. In Experiment 1 each student both restudied one passage and took a recall test on the other, then took a final free-recall test after 5 minutes, 2 days or 1 week. After 5 minutes the restudied passage won, 81% against 75%, t(39) = 3.22, d = 0.52. After 2 days the tested passage won, 68% against 54%, t(39) = 6.97, d = 0.95. After 1 week it won 56% against 42%, t(39) = 6.41, d = 0.83. The tested passage at one week was recalled about as well as the restudied passage at two days. Experiment 2 assigned 30 students to each of six cells and compared four study periods (SSSS), three study periods and one test (SSST), and one study period and three tests (STTT). At 5 minutes the order followed reading: 83%, 78%, 71%. At 1 week it inverted: 40%, 56%, 61%. STTT beat SSSS by t(58) = 4.78, d = 1.26, while STTT beat SSST only marginally, t(58) = 1.21, d = 0.31. Students in SSSS had read the passage 14.2 times on average and those in STTT 3.4 times. The questionnaire is the interesting part. Asked on a 7-point scale how well they would remember the passage in a week, SSSS students said 4.8, SSST 4.2 and STTT 4.0, F(2, 177) = 6.09. The group most confident of remembering was the group that remembered least. Karpicke and Roediger's 2008 Science experiment made the point in a harsher form. Students learned 40 Swahili-English word pairs, and once a pair had been recalled correctly it was either kept in both study and test cycles, dropped from study, dropped from test, or dropped from both. The four conditions produced the same learning curves and the same predictions, around 50% recall in a week, with condition means of 20.8, 20.4, 22.0 and 20.3 pairs. A week later the two conditions that kept testing recalled about 80% and the two that dropped testing recalled 36% and 33%. Combining them gave d = 4.03 with no overlap between the distributions. Restudying a pair after it had been recalled once bought nothing at all.

replication.headline: Rowland's 159 laboratory effect sizes against restudy controls give g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.42, 0.58]. Yang's 222 classroom studies give g = 0.499 against mixed controls, but only g = 0.330 where the control class restudied.
replication.detail: Rowland pooled 159 effect sizes from 61 studies reported between 1975 and 2013, every one of them a test condition against a restudy condition. The random-effects estimate was g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.42, 0.58], Z = 12.38, p < .001, with heterogeneity high at tau-squared = 0.21 and I-squared = 84.35. The unweighted mean was 0.54 and the median 0.55. Of the 159 effects, 81% favoured testing, 18% favoured restudy and 1% were zero. Published studies gave 0.58, 95% CI [0.49, 0.67], and unpublished ones 0.25, 95% CI [0.10, 0.41]; Rowland attributed the gap to design rather than suppression, since 89% of the unpublished effects used no feedback. He declined to apply the usual funnel-plot corrections, arguing that they mislead when heterogeneity is as high as it was here. Delay mattered as the theory predicts: 0.69, 95% CI [0.56, 0.81] at a day or more against 0.41, 95% CI [0.31, 0.51] under a day. Yang and colleagues asked the separate question of what happens in real classrooms, pooling 573 effects from 222 studies covering 48,478 students. The overall figure was g = 0.499, 95% CI [0.442, 0.557], with 82.9% of effects positive, and five bias checks including PET-PEESE, trim-and-fill and a three-parameter selection model found little to correct; the most pessimistic adjustment gave 0.427, 95% CI [0.395, 0.458]. Rowland excluded classroom studies by design and Yang reports that only 11% of the 272 effects in Adesope's meta-analysis came from classrooms, so the two literatures are close to disjoint. A third meta-analysis narrows the domain. Murray, Horner and Göbel pooled mathematics studies in 2025 and found 7 studies and 32 effect sizes comparing testing against restudy, with a weighted mean of g = 0.18 whose 95% interval crossed zero, which they read as no consistent retrieval-practice benefit for mathematics. Those figures come from the published abstract, because the full text could not be obtained; the OSF preprint of the same paper reports g = 0.22 from 6 studies and 20 effect sizes, so the two versions differ. No registered replication and no multi-site replication of the core effect was found in a search on 17 August 2026 of Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, the FORRT Replication Database and the open web.

study.cite: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432-1463.

limits: The laboratory number and the classroom number look identical and are not measuring the same thing. Rowland's 0.50 is testing against restudy. Yang's 0.499 is class quizzing against whatever the control class did, and that control turns out to be most of the effect. Split by control strategy, quizzing beat no activity or a filler task by g = 0.610, 95% CI [0.547, 0.673], beat restudying by g = 0.330, 95% CI [0.256, 0.404], and beat other elaborative strategies by g = 0.095, 95% CI [-0.005, 0.194], p = .062. Against an active alternative in a classroom the advantage is not reliable. Three further boundaries are in the meta-analytic tables. Retrieval that fails does nothing: with no feedback and initial recall at or below 50%, Rowland found g = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.27], p = .79, against 0.56, 95% CI [0.42, 0.70] above 75%. Feedback roughly doubles the effect, 0.73 against 0.39 in Rowland and 0.537 against 0.374 in Yang, so the no-feedback version is the weak version rather than the pure one. And quizzes given before teaching gave g = 0.186 in Yang against 0.536 after it. Durability in the field is less impressive than in the laboratory. Roediger, Agarwal, McDaniel and McDermott ran three experiments in a real sixth-grade social studies course. Their second enrolled 143 pupils and analysed 63, after dropping 23 in special-education or gifted programmes and 56 who missed a session. On chapter exams, quizzed items scored 91% against 83% for items read three times, t(62) = 6.61, d = 0.83. On an unanticipated semester exam three to five months later the same comparison was 59% against 53%, and the main effect of learning condition was not significant. Whether the effect survives complex material is disputed. Van Gog and Sweller argued in 2015 that it decreases or disappears as element interactivity rises; Karpicke and Aue replied in the same issue that element interactivity is not defined in a measurable way, that none of the worked-example experiments manipulated it, and that the null results came from the retrieval tasks used. Rowland's own stimulus moderator puts prose at 0.58, 95% CI [0.34, 0.82], above single words at 0.33, 95% CI [0.16, 0.50]. He adds that in his high-exposure subset, which keeps only studies with feedback or initial recall above 75%, single words matched prose and paired associates, so part of that gap is a gap in retrieval success. The effect has also failed to appear online. Sigayret, Parmentier and Silvestre ran two experiments on Prolific in 2026 and found no delayed-test difference, F(1, 66) = 0.13, p = 0.72 in the first and U = 1773, p = 0.17 in the second. Attrition was heavy, 67 of 169 recruits finishing the first and 129 of 426 the second, and the authors read the nulls as a limit on crowdsourced samples rather than on the effect. Evidence about lower-ability learners is thin. Agarwal and colleagues found retrieval-practice benefits larger for lower working-memory students in one of four cells, r = -.42 in the 39 students tested with feedback at two days, and no association in the other three. Zheng, Sun and Liu, analysing 30 of 35 Xiamen University undergraduates learning novel shapes paired with words, found the reverse: higher-capacity students showed the effect throughout, and lower-capacity ones only with familiar stimuli. Adesope, Trevisan and Sundararajan's 2017 meta-analysis, the other standard reference, is paywalled. Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and ERIC all recorded it as closed with no repository copy on 17 August 2026, and its abstract at Crossref carries no effect sizes, so nothing from it is quoted here at first hand.
misreadings: The most common error is the one the 2006 paper itself warns against. Testing did not beat restudying at every delay: at 5 minutes restudy won, 81% to 75%. But the opposite over-correction is also wrong, because Rowland's pooled estimate under one day is still 0.41, 95% CI [0.31, 0.51]. The crossover is a finding about one pair of experiments, not a law about short intervals. The second error is treating d = 4.03 from the Science paper as the size of the testing effect. That figure comes from a design in which one group stopped being tested on a word pair the moment it was recalled once, and the meta-analytic estimates sit near 0.5. Popular accounts also tend to quote whichever moderator suits them, and the two large meta-analyses disagree about moderators. Rowland found feedback doubled the effect; Yang reports that Adesope's meta-analysis found no feedback moderation, 0.63 with against 0.60 without. Rowland found the number of initial tests made no reliable difference; Yang reports Adesope finding a larger effect for one test, 0.70, than for more than one, 0.51, while Yang's own classroom data run the other way, 0.444 for one quiz rising to 0.762 for unlimited attempts. Those Adesope figures are quoted here from Yang's description of that paper and not from the paper. A separate claim, that retrieval practice beats concept mapping, has been undercut. Mayrhofer, Kuhbandner and Frischholz ran a preregistered study of 230 participants and found that the advantage held only while the concept-mapping condition lacked the extra memorisation phase the retrieval condition received, and vanished, p = 0.854, once both groups memorised. The last misreading is that students already know all this. Karpicke, Butler and Roediger asked 177 undergraduates to list their study strategies. Rereading was named by 84% and ranked first by 55%; practising recall was named by 11%, 19 of 177, and ranked first by 1%, 2 of 177. Asked to choose between rereading a chapter and trying to recall it, 57% of 101 students chose to reread and 18% chose to self-test. The other 76 students got the same question with restudy allowed after the test, and 42% of them chose to test themselves. Of those 76, 30% wanted the feedback to guide more studying and 3% believed the act of recall would itself help them remember.
